newsitem.title: USA: Republican gives some support to U.S. EPA air plan.
newsitem.headline: Republican gives some support to U.S. EPA air plan.

text.p: A leading moderate Republican said Tuesday he believed that studies supported the Environmental Protection Agency's proposal to tighten air quality standards.

"I think there are some compelling data that lead one to conclude that the EPA is not way off base" on its proposed standards for smog and soot pollution, Rep Sherwood Boehlert, who co-chairs a House Republican task force on the environment, told an environmental policy group.
But the New York Republican said that Environment and Public Works Committee Chairman John Chafee had raised legitimate concerns that the tougher standards would strain states' resources.
"I think that my colleague, friend, ally and soulmate John Chafee has also raised some legitimate questions that need to be addressed," Boehlert said.

Chafee, of Rhode Island, also has said the soot rule would have greater health effects and should be a priority, but that there still were "important gaps in our knowledge" of how very small particles impair health.

"I support EPA's efforts to control the smallest particulates that present a threat to public health. My concern is that focusing on size alone, like the 1987 standard did, will miss the mark again and result in another ten years of misdirected pollution controls that fail to protect public health," Chafee said in a letter earlier this month to the American Lung Association.
In his remarks, Boehlert said he did not expect Congress to vote on the EPA smog and ozone standards until after the EPA issues its final rule on them in June.

A law passed last year sets up a procedure for Congress to review and vote on regulations. The president still would have the power to veto a congressional vote, then Congress would have to muster the votes to override the veto.
A number of congressional committees plan hearings on the issue which has been called the EPA's biggest regulatory proposal ever.
Several congressmen have said they doubted that the health benefits would justify the large economic costs of meeting the stricter standards.
